docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Do you develop, maintain or use open source software (OSS) on your AUVs, ASVs, ROVs, etc.?

Open Ocean Software would like to invite you to our first community day at the National Oceanography Centre in Southampton, UK, where you can expect focused talks, in-depth discussions, and plenty of time for networking in a single-track format. This is also your chance to have early feedback on the goals and implementation of the Open Ocean Software organization.

Open Ocean Software is a new initiative to support building ecosystems around OSS for marine robots to improve technical quality, security, maintainability, documentation, interoperability, and to build a vibrant human community around the topic. Open Ocean Software is led by a team of collaborators who have collectively spent decades deploying AUVs in diverse real-world environments running a range of OSS projects. We are currently funded by the US National Science Foundation under the Pathways to Enable Open-Source Ecosystems (POSE) initiative.

This workshop will take place on Friday, 4 September 2026, directly following the IEEE OES AUV Symposium, also held in Southampton.

docs.title: Call for Presentation Abstracts
docs.text:
We invite you to submit an abstract for a technical talk using the link below. These abstracts will be reviewed by the technical committee and accepted talks will be included in one of these tracks:

  • Lightning talk [CLOSED]: A very brief talk intended to introduce the audience to your topic for fruitful discussions later in the day and beyond.
  • Standard talk [CLOSED: abstracts were due 17 July]: A standard-length conference talk focusing on your development or use of open source in your marine robotics work.

We are interested in a wide range of topics that both include open source software, and applies to marine robots or related technologies: sensors, data acquisition, simulation, and more.

You do not need to be an author of the OSS project to present how it has been useful (or not) to your application. Also, we are interested in learning from failures, false starts, and critiques as much as successes.

docs.title: Join as a member project
docs.text:
Your project keeps its code, roadmap and home page. We list it in the directory and on the forum, and once it has tagged releases we can package it in the signed apt repository.

Start on the forum Read the standards (PDF)

You provide Source in git, a working build and install (CMake for C/C++, pyproject.toml for Python, etc.), and a tagged release schedule.

docs.title: Minimum standards
docs.text:
We ask what your documentation and process must answer, not which tool writes it. A README, docstrings, tests, or a paper appendix all count.

Plus a published OSI-approved license.

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
1. Purpose. What the component does and its intended scope.
  2. Usage. At least one minimal, realistic example.
  3. Interface. Inputs, outputs, expected behavior, and failure modes.
  4. Assumptions and constraints. Preconditions, units, coordinate frames, timing.

docs.title: Maintainability
docs.text:
1. Build reproducibility. A contributor can build from a clean state with documented steps.
  2. Interface contracts. Message formats, types, units, and frames are stated.
  3. Verified behavior. Tests, a runnable example, or a manual validation procedure.
  4. Issue visibility. A public way to report defects and see known issues.

docs.title: Maintainability badges
docs.text:
A badge tells users what to expect. Each level lists the minimum standard, the DevOps help we offer to reach it, and well-known open-source projects at that level.

Research-GradeCommunity-GradeProject-GradeProduct-GradeEcosystem-Grade

Standard: builds from documented steps on at least one known platform. Some evidence of tested behavior. Issues reportable via any channel.

DevOps: builds locally. No CI or packaging required.

Examples: many code releases that accompany academic papers.

Standard: clean build from documented steps. At least one automated test or runnable example. Public issue tracker. Interface inputs and outputs documented.

DevOps: CI on the primary platform. Dockerfile available.

Examples: MOOS-IvP, MAVLink.

Standard: CI runs on changes. Interfaces formally defined and tested. Installable on at least one target platform. Contributing and issue guidelines published.

DevOps: multi-platform CI. Packages in the shared repository. Multi-arch Docker images.

Examples: ROS 2 core packages, ArduSub.

Standard: multi-platform packaging. Full regression suite. Schema-validated configuration. Changelog and deprecation policy.

DevOps: integration tests with other member projects. Release automation.

Examples: ArduPilot, PX4.

Standard: formal compatibility guarantees across platforms and versions. Governed CI infrastructure. Long-term support commitments.

DevOps: cross-project CI. Shared build infrastructure. Reproducible deployment stacks.

Examples: ROS 2 full ecosystem, Linux kernel.

docs.title: Research code is welcome
docs.text:
The standards explicitly support research and experimental software. For Research-Grade projects these are acceptable:

  • Manual validation in place of automated tests
  • Source-only distribution with documented build workarounds
  • One known-good platform instead of broad portability
  • Interface contracts documented in a paper or README section

docs.title: How to apply
docs.text:
1. Introduce the project. Post on the forum. Maintainers can apply; users can nominate a project they depend on.
  2. Self-assess. Link evidence for the eight minimums and your license.
  3. Peer review. Member maintainers review and agree on a stage and badge.
  4. Onboard. Your project page goes live in the directory, and we start on packaging.

Start on the forum

docs.title: Channels
docs.text:
Packages are published to three channels, each its own set of apt repositories:

Channel Contents Signed with Projects Release Tagged releases, published after a reviewer approves Release key MOOS-IvP, Goby3, DCCL, NETSIM Beta Tagged prereleases Release key openocean-messages Continuous The latest trusted commit on each project's main branch Continuous key Goby3, DCCL, NETSIM, IvPico, the IvP Helm libraries without MOOS, openocean-messages

The release channel also carries the dependencies these projects need that Debian and Ubuntu don't package (MAVLink, libais, Wt).

docs.title: Install from apt.oceansoft.org
docs.text:
Trust

These instructions assume oceansoft.org and the openocean-build repository haven't been compromised (and thus list the correct GPG fingerprints). This is normally a safe assumption, but if your security requirements call for it, consider independently verifying our signing key, e.g. using Keybase or other out-of-band techniques.

For Debian bookworm and trixie, and Ubuntu jammy, noble and resolute, on amd64 and arm64. A few projects skip a release whose dependencies are too old.

Setup scriptBy hand

apt-setup adds the release channel, checking the key's fingerprint before apt is told to trust it:

curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openocean-software/openocean-build/main/scripts/apt-setup

sudo bash apt-setup

Options add more: --beta and --continuous for those channels, and --zenoh for Eclipse Zenoh's repository, which goby3-zenoh needs.

  • Get the release key and check its fingerprint (details): 
    OOS_KEY=D7D7224D53A4F29E303FE01DEB505B68A5D063B0
OOS_KEYRING=/usr/share/keyrings/openocean-release.asc
curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/openocean-software/openocean-build/main/keys/release.asc
gpg --show-keys --with-colons release.asc | grep -x "fpr:::::::::$OOS_KEY:" && sudo install -m 0644 release.asc $OOS_KEYRING
  • Add apt sources: 
    DISTRO=$(. /etc/os-release; echo "$ID")             # "ubuntu" or "debian"
DIST=$(. /etc/os-release; echo "$VERSION_CODENAME") # e.g., "resolute"
printf 'Types: deb\nURIs: https://apt.oceansoft.org/release/%s-%s\nSuites: %s\nComponents: main\nSigned-By: %s\n' \
  $DISTRO $DIST $DIST $OOS_KEYRING | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/openocean-release.sources
sudo apt update

The beta channel is the same with beta in place of release in the URL. The continuous channel also needs its own key. See Installing packages.

Then:

  • Install packages: 

    sudo apt install ...

  • Full list of packages available: 

    sudo apt install lz4
lz4cat /var/lib/apt/lists/apt.oceansoft.org*_Packages.lz4 | grep '^Package:'

Set up before November 2026?

The repositories moved from apt.oceansoft.org/<distro>-<dist>/ to apt.oceansoft.org/release/<distro>-<dist>. Remove /etc/apt/sources.list.d/oceansoft.list and /etc/apt/keyrings/oceansoft.gpg, then follow the steps above.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Dynamic Compact Control Language (DCCL) is a language for marshalling (or roughly analogously: source encoding or compressing) object-based messages for extremely low throughput network links. Originally designed for commanding and retrieving data from autonomous underwater vehicles over acoustic modem links, DCCL has found additional uses in the robotics community, such as for sending messages over satellite or degraded land-based links.

It is suitable when a very small encoded message size matters much more than the speed of encoding and decoding. Goby3 uses DCCL for its intervehicle layer.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Signed binary packages for Debian and Ubuntu, built by the Open Ocean pipeline from signed DCCL release tags. Packaging lives in openocean-build.

  1. Add the Open Ocean apt repository and signing key: follow the apt setup steps on the Toolkit page.

  2. Install the command line tools, the development files and the Python bindings:

    sudo apt install dccl5-apps libdccl5-dev python3-dccl5

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
Package Contents libdccl5, libdccl5-dev Library and development files dccl5-compiler protoc plugin dccl5-apps Command line tools, including dccl python3-dccl5 Python bindings dccl5-doc Documentation

Prereleases go to the beta channel, and builds of the latest commit to the continuous channel; see channels.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Goby Underwater Autonomy Project aims to create a unified framework for autonomous marine vehicle collaboration, seamlessly incorporating efficient intervehicle (acoustic, satellite, etc.), flexible interprocess (ethernet, local sockets, etc.), and intuitive interthread (shared pointer) communications. Goby also provides tools for interacting with other marine-related middleware, as well as marine engineering and oceanographic data.

Goby3 uses DCCL to encode messages for low-throughput links.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Signed binary packages for Debian and Ubuntu, built by the Open Ocean pipeline from signed Goby3 release tags. Packaging lives in openocean-build.

  1. Add the Open Ocean apt repository and signing key: follow the apt setup steps on the Toolkit page. For the Zenoh transport, run the setup script with --zenoh.

  2. Install the applications and the development files:

    sudo apt install goby3-apps libgoby3-dev

docs.text:
Package Contents goby3-apps, goby3-gui Applications, and the GUI applications libgoby3, libgoby3-dev, libgoby3-gui-dev Libraries and development files goby3-moos, libgoby3-moos, libgoby3-moos-dev MOOS middleware connections goby3-zenoh, libgoby3-zenoh, libgoby3-zenoh-dev Zenoh transport python3-goby3, goby3-julia Python and Julia support goby3-clang-tool, goby3-interfaces goby_clang_tool and the interface definition files goby3-doc, goby3-test Documentation and unit tests

The continuous channel carries builds of the latest commit.

docs.title: Connects with
docs.text: Stack Bridge Notes MOOS-IvP Mature Built into Goby3. Translates between Goby pub/sub and MOOSDB variables. ROS 2 Demo goby_ros_gateway bridges the Goby3 interprocess layer to ROS 2 topics. Not yet used outside the original demo code.

Signed binary packages for Debian and Ubuntu, built by the Open Ocean pipeline from tagged MOOS-IvP releases. Packaging lives in openocean-build.

  1. Add the Open Ocean apt repository and signing key: follow the apt setup steps on the Toolkit page.

  2. Install the helm, apps, and GUI tools:

    sudo apt install moos-ivp-apps moos-ivp-gui moos-ivp-tools

The IvP Helm libraries built without MOOS (libivp-helm0, libivp-helm-dev) are in the continuous channel, as snapshots until a MOOS-IvP release includes that build option. They install beside libmoos-ivp.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
ros_acomms is a ROS package that provides a generic ROS interface to the WHOI Micromodem and transparent transport of ROS messages across an acoustic link. It also provides simulation capabilities.

The same packages build under ROS 1 (catkin) and ROS 2 (ament). Source is on the WHOI GitLab, and the documentation covers setup and the simulator.

docs.title: License
docs.text: Message, service and launch definitions are LGPL-3.0. The nodes and the rest of the code are AGPL-3.0. The repo's LICENSE gives the reason: groups that change ros_acomms should contribute those changes back.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
WHOI-ROS is a collection of shared ROS 2 software libraries and tools developed by the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution for underwater vehicle operations.

It is the next-generation evolution of WHOI robotics software, migrated from the earlier DS_ROS (Deep Submergence ROS) framework. Source is on the WHOI GitLab.
